q: In a chemical equation, the sign ⇌ shows that the reaction is:
x: The double half-arrow shows that the reaction can go both ways: reactants form products and products re-form reactants.

q: At chemical equilibrium, which quantity is zero?
o: The rate of the forward reaction
The rate of the reverse reaction
x: Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the net rate (forward minus reverse) is zero. Neither individual rate is zero.

q: Which of these reactions is reversible under ordinary conditions in a closed vessel?
o: Precipitation of AgCl from AgNO₃ and NaCl solutions
x: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ readily goes both ways and sets up an equilibrium. The other three go practically to completion.

q: CaCO₃ heated in an open vessel decomposes completely, but in a closed vessel it reaches equilibrium. The reason is that in the closed vessel:
o: The temperature cannot rise high enough
No CO₂ is formed at all
CO₂ cannot escape, so it recombines with CaO
x: CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂. In an open vessel CO₂ escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot occur; in a closed vessel it stays and re-forms CaCO₃.

q: When a reversible reaction is started with reactants only, the rate of the reverse reaction at the very start is:
x: No products are present at the start, so the reverse reaction cannot occur yet. Its rate rises as products build up.

q: On a graph of concentration against time for a reversible reaction in a closed vessel, equilibrium is reached when:
o: The curves for reactants and products become flat (horizontal)
The curves for reactants and products cross each other
All the curves fall to zero
The product curve rises above the reactant curve
x: At equilibrium, concentrations stop changing, so their curves level off. They need not be equal, so crossing does not mark equilibrium.

q: Which of these claims about a system at equilibrium is NOT true?
o: It can be reached from either the reactant side or the product side
It is set up only in a closed system
The concentrations stay constant at constant temperature
At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions stop
x: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions go on at equal rates. The other three statements are true.

q: For X ⇌ Y, the rate constants of the forward and reverse reactions are kf and kr. At equilibrium, Kc equals:
x: At equilibrium, kf[X] = kr[Y], so Kc = [Y]/[X] = kf/kr.

q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the reverse reaction is:
o: The combination of H₂ and I₂ to form HI
The burning of hydrogen in iodine vapour
The decomposition of HI into H₂ and I₂
The ionisation of HI in water
x: The reverse reaction runs right to left: 2HI → H₂ + I₂. Combination of H₂ and I₂ is the forward reaction.

q: At constant temperature, a reaction mixture in a closed vessel has reached equilibrium when its:
o: Reactants have all been used up
Colour, pressure and concentrations no longer change
x: At equilibrium, measurable (macroscopic) properties such as colour, pressure and concentration become constant, though both reactions continue.

q: The Kc expression for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) is:
x: Kc = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient: [N₂O₄]/[NO₂]². Coefficients are powers, not multipliers.

q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at equilibrium, [N₂O₄] = 0.1 and [NO₂] = 0.2 mol dm⁻³. The value of Kc is:
x: Kc = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] = (0.2)²/0.1 = 0.04/0.1 = 0.4 mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the square gives 2.

q: 1 mol of CO and 1 mol of H₂O(g) are heated in a 1 dm³ closed vessel: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂. At equilibrium 0.75 mol of CO₂ is present. The value of Kc is:
x: At equilibrium CO₂ = H₂ = 0.75 and CO = H₂O = 0.25 mol dm⁻³. Kc = (0.75 × 0.75)/(0.25 × 0.25) = 9.

q: For which reaction is Kp equal to Kc?
x: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, so they are equal when Δn = 0. For N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO there are 2 mol of gas on each side.

q: For a reaction mixture, the reaction quotient Qc is found to be greater than Kc. The mixture will:
o: Undergo net forward reaction until Qc rises to Kc
Stay unchanged, as it is already at equilibrium
Change its Kc value to match Qc
Undergo net reverse reaction until Qc falls to Kc
x: Qc > Kc means there are too many products for equilibrium, so net reverse reaction occurs. Kc is fixed at a given temperature.

q: In the law of mass action, the active mass of a substance in solution is taken as its:
x: Active mass means molar concentration, written in square brackets, e.g. [H₂]. The rate is proportional to the product of active masses.

q: N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) has ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹. The equilibrium yield of NO is increased by:
x: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating shifts the equilibrium to the right. Moles of gas are equal on both sides, so pressure has no effect, and a catalyst never changes the yield.

q: Extra chlorine gas is pumped into a vessel holding PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at equilibrium, keeping volume and temperature fixed. What follows?
o: The equilibrium shifts to the right and more PCl₃ forms
The equilibrium shifts to the left and more PCl₅ forms
x: Adding a product makes the system use some of it up, so the reverse reaction is favoured. Kc does not change at constant temperature.

q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), the volume of the vessel is increased at constant temperature, lowering the pressure. The equilibrium:
o: Shifts to the left, towards fewer gas molecules
Shifts to the right, towards more gas molecules
Does not shift, as Kc is unchanged
Shifts to the left and Kc decreases
x: Lower pressure favours the side with more moles of gas: 2 on the right against 1 on the left, so more PCl₅ dissociates.

q: Fe³⁺ (yellow) + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺ (blood red). When more Fe³⁺ ions are added, the colour of the solution:
x: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, forming more red FeSCN²⁺.

q: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g), ΔH negative. The equilibrium yield of methanol is greatest at:
x: 3 mol of gas give 1 mol, so high pressure favours methanol; the forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature also favours it.

q: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) in a closed vessel, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:
o: To the left, as the only gas is on the right
To the right, as more solid forms
Not at all, as solids are present
To the right, as Kc increases
x: Only CO₂ is a gas, and it is on the right. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, so CaCO₃ re-forms.

q: C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g) has ΔH positive. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of H₂?
x: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating favours it. Higher pressure favours the left (1 gas mol against 2), removing steam shifts it left, and a catalyst has no effect on yield.

q: Extra reactant is added to an equilibrium mixture at constant temperature. After equilibrium is re-established, the value of Kc:
x: Changing a concentration shifts the position of equilibrium, but Kc changes only with temperature.

q: A saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt is one in which:
o: No undissolved solid can ever be present
The dissolved ions are in equilibrium with the undissolved solid
The ionic product is less than Ksp
x: In a saturated solution, solid dissolves and ions re-crystallise at equal rates, so the ionic product equals Ksp.

q: The Ksp expression for aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃, is:
x: Al(OH)₃ ⇌ Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻, so Ksp = [Al³⁺][OH⁻]³. The coefficient becomes a power.

q: A metal hydroxide M(OH)₂ has Ksp = 4 × 10⁻¹² at 25 °C. How many moles of it dissolve per dm³ of pure water?
x: If s mol dissolve, [M²⁺] = s and [OH⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = 4s³ = 4 × 10⁻¹². s³ = 1 × 10⁻¹², s = 1 × 10⁻⁴. Treating it as a 1 : 1 salt gives 2 × 10⁻⁶.

q: At 25 °C, Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. A solution has [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹². This solution is:
o: Already holding the maximum dissolved AgCl
x: The ionic product 1 × 10⁻¹² is less than Ksp 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so the solution is unsaturated and more AgCl could dissolve.

q: The units of Ksp for AgCl are:
x: Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = (mol dm⁻³)(mol dm⁻³) = mol² dm⁻⁶.

q: The concentration of the undissolved solid is not included in a Ksp expression because:
o: The concentration of a pure solid is constant
The solid does not take part in the equilibrium
x: The solid does take part in the equilibrium, but its concentration (its density over its molar mass) is constant, so it is absorbed into Ksp.

q: Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and Ksp of Ag₂CrO₄ is 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Which statement about their molar solubilities in water is correct?
o: Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble, since Ksp = 4s³ gives the larger s
AgCl is more soluble, since its Ksp value is larger
Both are equally soluble, since both are silver salts
Neither dissolves at all, since both Ksp values are tiny
x: AgCl: s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵. Ag₂CrO₄: s = ∛(1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4) ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵, so Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble. Ksp values compare solubility directly only for salts of the same formula type.

q: Suppression of a salt's solubility by adding an ion it already contains is explained by:
x: Adding an ion already present in an equilibrium shifts it to use up that ion, as Le Chatelier's principle predicts.

q: A little HCl is added to a solution of ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH). The degree of ionisation of the ethanoic acid:
o: Increases, because HCl supplies more H⁺
Stays the same, because HCl is a strong acid
Increases, because CH₃COO⁻ ions are removed
Decreases, because of the common H⁺ ion
x: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺. Extra H⁺ from HCl shifts this to the left, so less ethanoic acid ionises.

q: In soap making, common salt (NaCl) is added to make the soap (a sodium salt of a fatty acid) separate out. This works because:
o: NaCl reacts with the soap to form a new compound
NaCl raises the boiling point of the mixture
The common Na⁺ ion lowers the solubility of the soap
Cl⁻ ions break the soap down into fatty acid
x: This is called salting out: the extra Na⁺ ions push the solubility equilibrium of the sodium soap back, so the soap separates.

q: The solubility of lead(II) chloride, PbCl₂, in water is lowered by adding:
x: KCl supplies Cl⁻, an ion common to PbCl₂, which shifts PbCl₂ ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ to the left. Nitrates share no ion with PbCl₂.

q: Ksp of Mg(OH)₂ is 1 × 10⁻¹¹. If [OH⁻] is fixed at 0.1 mol dm⁻³ by dissolved NaOH, the concentration of Mg²⁺ that can remain in solution is:
x: Ksp = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]², so [Mg²⁺] = 1 × 10⁻¹¹/(0.1)² = 1 × 10⁻⁹. Forgetting to square [OH⁻] gives 1 × 10⁻¹⁰.

q: Adding which substance to a solution of ethanoic acid would NOT suppress its ionisation?
x: NaCl supplies neither H⁺ nor CH₃COO⁻, so it has no common ion with ethanoic acid. The other three each supply one of these ions.

q: When the solubility of a salt is lowered by adding a common ion at constant temperature, its Ksp:
x: Solubility falls, but Ksp is a constant at a given temperature; the ion concentrations simply readjust so their product still equals Ksp.

q: A buffer made from ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate has a pH that is:
x: A weak acid with its salt forms an acidic buffer; with similar amounts its pH is near the pKa of ethanoic acid, 4.74.

q: For an acidic buffer, the Henderson equation is:
x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). More salt raises the pH; when [salt] = [acid], pH = pKa.

q: A weak acid HX has pKa = 5.0. A buffer contains 0.2 mol dm⁻³ HX and 0.02 mol dm⁻³ NaX. Its pH is:
x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 5.0 + log(0.02/0.2) = 5.0 + log(0.1) = 5.0 − 1 = 4.0. Inverting the ratio gives 6.0.

q: A buffer can also be made from two salts of a polyprotic acid. Which mixture is such a buffer?
x: H₂PO₄⁻ acts as a weak acid and HPO₄²⁻ as its conjugate base, so the pair resists pH change. The other pairs are neutral salts of strong acids and bases.

q: The buffer capacity of a CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa buffer is greatest when:
x: A buffer resists added acid and added base best when the acid and its salt are present in equal amounts (pH = pKa). Without either one, it cannot buffer at all.

q: A CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa buffer is diluted with an equal volume of water. Its pH:
o: Falls sharply, because the acid becomes stronger
Rises to 7, because water is neutral
Halves, because both concentrations are halved
Stays almost the same, because the ratio [salt]/[acid] is unchanged
x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]); dilution halves both concentrations, so the ratio and hence the pH hardly change.

q: Which mixture, after reaction in water, gives a buffer solution?
x: 0.1 mol NaOH turns half the acid into CH₃COONa, leaving 0.1 mol CH₃COOH with 0.1 mol CH₃COO⁻: a buffer. Equal moles of acid and NaOH leave only salt; HCl and NaOH give no weak acid.

q: In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen are fed to the converter in the volume ratio:
x: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, so the gases are mixed in the ratio of the equation, 1 volume of N₂ to 3 volumes of H₂.

q: The formation of ammonia, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, is:
o: Endothermic, ΔH ≈ +92 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
Exothermic, ΔH ≈ −46 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
Exothermic, ΔH ≈ −92 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
Endothermic, ΔH ≈ +46 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
x: About 92 kJ of heat is given out per 2 mol of NH₃ (46 kJ per mole), so the reaction is exothermic. This is why high temperature lowers the yield.

q: Removing ammonia from the equilibrium mixture N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ causes:
o: The equilibrium to shift to the left
More N₂ and H₂ to combine, as the equilibrium shifts to the right
No change in the amounts of N₂ and H₂
x: Removing a product makes the system replace it, so more N₂ and H₂ react. Kc stays the same at constant temperature.

q: At the same temperature and pressure, 30 dm³ of hydrogen reacts completely with excess nitrogen. The volume of ammonia formed is:
x: 3 volumes of H₂ give 2 volumes of NH₃, so 30 dm³ H₂ gives 30 × 2/3 = 20 dm³ NH₃.

q: Most of the ammonia made by the Haber process is used to manufacture:
o: Fertilisers such as urea and ammonium salts
x: The main use of ammonia is in nitrogen fertilisers such as urea, ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulphate.

q: A catalyst is still needed in the Haber process at 400–500 °C because:
o: The catalyst increases the yield of ammonia
Hydrogen does not react with anything without it
The strong N≡N triple bond gives the reaction a high activation energy
x: Breaking the very strong N≡N bond needs a lot of energy, so the reaction is slow even when hot; the iron catalyst lowers the activation energy. It does not change the yield.

q: If the Haber process were run at 700 °C instead of about 450 °C, the result would be:
o: A slower rate and a lower equilibrium yield
A faster rate but a lower equilibrium yield of ammonia
A faster rate and a higher equilibrium yield
A slower rate but a higher equilibrium yield
x: A higher temperature always speeds up the reaction, but the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left and less ammonia is present.
